p.x:
Every morning, my house is very busy. First, Mum turns on the radio. Dad puts the dirty clothes in the washing machine. In winter, we turn on the heater because it's cold.
My brother always looks for the remote control. He wants to watch cartoons! I plug my phone charger into the wall because my battery is low. The cable is very short, so I sit on the floor.
Then the doorbell rings. It's our neighbour with a cake. What a nice surprise!

Our homes are full of machines. Most families have a dishwasher, a vacuum cleaner and an air conditioner. Today, many of these are becoming "smart". In a smart home, you can control appliances with an app on your phone.
For example, you can turn on the air conditioner before you get home, or ask a smart speaker to play music, read the news or tell you the weather. With a simple voice command, you can switch off the lights. A robot vacuum can clean the floor while you are at work, and lights with a motion sensor switch on automatically when you walk into a room.
Smart homes can also save money. Energy-saving devices reduce your electricity bill, and automatic systems turn off appliances that aren't being used. Some homes even unlock the front door with a fingerprint.
Setting up a smart home is not always easy. You need a good router and some devices need to be plugged into a socket near it. You may have to read long instructions, and if something goes wrong, you might need to reset everything. However, most new devices are user-friendly. Many families enjoy watching films on a smart TV, and a few years ago this was high-tech, but now it's normal.

The internet of things refers to the growing network of everyday objects, from fridges to door locks, that are connected to the internet. Technology companies promise a future in which homes automate routine tasks, adjusting lighting, temperature and even shopping lists without human input. Keyless entry systems using face recognition already allow residents to open their doors without searching for keys, while remote access lets homeowners check security cameras from anywhere in the world.
This technology may be particularly valuable for older people. In assisted living, smart devices can remind residents to take medication, and a fall detector can automatically alert family members or emergency services if someone collapses. For many elderly people, such tools offer greater independence and allow them to remain in their own homes for longer.
However, critics raise serious concerns. Each connected device collects data about its users' habits, and some people fear that their voice assistants may spy on private conversations. Poorly protected devices can also be hacked, giving criminals access to home networks. Experts recommend changing default passwords, installing every software update promptly and learning how to configure privacy settings carefully.
The smart home may still seem futuristic to many, but it is rapidly becoming the norm. The challenge is to enjoy its convenience without sacrificing security and privacy.
